correctness.rationale: For all n>=k+2, one legal first force makes the complete closed neighborhood of its source blue; an interior interval of width 2k+1 can grow to an endpoint, and a blue prefix/suffix of length >=k+1 then grows to the opposite endpoint. Interior triggering supports are 2k-subsets of a 2k+1 consecutive window omitting a noncentral vertex: 2k-2 distinct internal-hole shifts plus one class of consecutive blocks. The count is (2k-1)(n-2k)+1. Factorial-moment overlaps occupy at least 2k+1 blue sites per nontrivial overlap component and contribute o(1) when p=c n^(-1/(2k)). A boundary-force error O_k(p^k) and missing-site error O_k(n p^(2k+1)) vanish. Full brute-force simulation compared 24456 initial assignments with an independently written first-force checker. Direct motif census matched 20 parameters. A distinct weighted finite-state enumeration produced three probabilities approaching the rigorously proven square-path limit.

originality.rationale: The closest primary graph-power result gives only minimum seed cardinality, and the random-set paper gives general comparisons and the ordinary path threshold, not the complete distributional law for all fixed path powers. An accessible earlier exact optimal-set classification only describes smallest-cardinality seed sets, whereas the new critical window arises from a linear number of distinct 2k-site interior trigger supports. The standard rare-local-pattern Poisson principle does not itself establish the structural first-force equivalence or the model-dependent exact constant. value.rationale: Random-set zero forcing is a motivated threshold problem, and zero forcing of graph powers has an active 2026 primary literature. This result determines the exact finite-size scaling window, the limiting distribution and the half-success constant for every fixed k>=2, rather than only deterministic minimum size or a rough threshold. The exact (2k-1)-motif explanation resolves a nontrivial double-counting of adjacent first-force events, and its proof supplies a structural deterministic equivalence useful for other seed distributions.
